sentence: Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, and the NHS says help is available when they affect daily life.
Often there is no underlying medical reason, though fibroids, endometriosis and some other conditions can cause heavy periods.

sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect life, have lasted some time, come with severe pain, or if there is bleeding between periods or after sex.
Treatment choices include some contraceptives, medicines to reduce bleeding and surgery, and heavy periods do not always need treatment.
note: Search summary of NHS inform pages

sentence: The NHS describes heavy periods in practical terms, such as needing to change pads or tampons every one to two hours.
note: NHS period problems page as summarised

sentence: Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, but the NHS says that when periods are so heavy that they affect life, help is available.
Feeling tired or short of breath, or avoiding daily activities because of periods, are other signs that bleeding may be a problem.
note: Search summary of NHS inform page

sentence: Heavy periods often have no underlying cause.
Fibroids, which are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb, are a common identifiable cause.

sentence: Other conditions that can cause heavy periods include endometriosis, adenomyosis, polycystic ovary syndrome and pelvic inflammatory disease.
note: Search summary of NHS inform and Wales pages

sentence: Some medicines, such as anticoagulants and some chemotherapy medicines, can also be responsible.
note: Search summary of NHS inform page

sentence: Rarely, heavy periods can be a sign of womb cancer.
NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect your life, have lasted for some time, or come with severe pain.
Bleeding between periods or after sex is also a reason to see a GP.
For severe period or pelvic pain that is worse than usual and not helped by painkillers, the NHS advises getting urgent advice, from NHS 111 if needed.
note: Search summary of NHS period pain page; page for this line is nhs.uk/symptoms/period-pain, not period problems

sentence: A GP can investigate why bleeding is heavy, which may include a physical examination, blood tests or scans.
A blood test to look for iron deficiency anaemia is usually offered to people with heavy periods.
A pregnancy test, an ultrasound scan and, less often, a hysteroscopy (a look inside the womb with a small camera) may follow.
note: Search summary; description of hysteroscopy is a gloss

sentence: Keeping a record of the bleeding before the appointment is suggested to help the discussion.
note: Search summary: a period diary is recommended

sentence: Heavy periods do not always need to be treated.
If they affect daily life, options include a hormone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS) or the combined contraceptive pill.
Medicines to reduce the bleeding, such as tranexamic acid, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as mefenamic acid or naproxen are also used.
Surgical options exist, and some treatments affect whether a person can become pregnant, so the clinician discusses this when treatment is chosen.
note: Search summary: some treatments affect fertility; discussion is a gloss

sentence: If treatments have not worked, or a condition may be causing the bleeding, a referral to a hospital specialist may follow.
